Yet by no means do all the stories of visions of, or approaches to, the Hidden Imam’s country require such a long journey beforehand. It is as though Nâ-kojâ-Âbâd—the place that is not contained within any place on the map of the world perceived by our senses—suddenly, fleetingly breaks into our world. Or, if we prefer, it makes itself present within the visionary’s inner world. We might equally say, looking at it the other way around, that the visionary suddenly enters it. The two descriptions come to the same thing. For its “where”—its ubi—in relation to our “where,” our place and position (situs) in this world, is an ubique: an “everywhere.”

Another kind of story shows us this, and we shall recount one particularly revealing example. The event was brief and astonishing; so is the account of it. Through these stories—and we could multiply the examples—we enter a world, or see a world manifest itself, that lies beyond the empirical reach of our senses and rational sciences. Were this not so, anyone could find the way into it and establish its existence by ordinary means.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02129

But we cannot even retrace the roads taken by the witnesses—and with good reason. Here the philosopher’s inquiry gathers around themes already brought to light: Nâ-kojâ-Âbâd; the imaginative faculty fully exercising the power of knowledge that properly belongs to it; and “the soul as the spiritual place of the body.”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02130

The testimony of eyewitnesses brings us face to face with a spiritual world—but a spiritual world that is concrete, richer in forms than our own, and whose forms are not subject to decay. (The marvelous cities of the five islands belong to the world of Jâbarsâ, the mundus imaginalis.) The question is ubi: where? Our philosophers’ understanding of how the spiritual world at the level of the Soul—that is, the Malakût, the realm of the soul—relates to the physical world accessible to our senses has already led us to a double answer: everywhere (ubique) and nowhere at once.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02131

This means that the Malakût can break into our sensory world at any point, and that we can enter it from any point, without the Malakût being located anywhere within that sensory world. Such a breakthrough, such an entry, requires the activity of a faculty that is neither sense perception nor abstract reasoning. What this subtle faculty perceives is neither fantasy nor the merely imaginary. The real events it allows us to experience belong neither to myth nor to history.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02132

We referred explicitly earlier to the Persian expression Nâ-kojâ-âbâd, coined by Suhrawardi, because when the Shaykh al-Ishrâq—the master of Illuminationist philosophy—uses this expression, he presupposes the entire understanding of being that gives it meaning. We have had several occasions to point this out in the course of this book. To come from Nâ-kojâ-âbâd is to come from beyond the cosmic mountain of Qâf. It is from there that the mysterious initiator, the angel who acts as a personal guide, declares himself to have come at the beginning of the initiatory tales of Avicenna and Suhrawardi. We know that in two of Suhrawardi’s tales the angel explicitly answers the person questioning him: “I come from Nâ-kojâ-âbâd.”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02133

And the reader will have encountered here, in Book II, in the Tale of the Crimson Archangel, what the Archangel suggests to his disciple about the meaning of “crossing the mountain of Qâf” and the path one must take to emerge beyond it. That tale also suggested that anyone who, like the mysterious prophet Khezr, had bathed in the Source of Life could make the crossing without difficulty. And now, in fact, we have met the prophet Khezr twice more: beside the Twelfth Imam in the story of the shaykh of Jam-Karân, and near the small temple on the Green Island where one can communicate with the Imam.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02134

Suhrawardi formed the strange expression Nâ-kojâ-âbâd—which is not found in Persian dictionaries—out of the resources of Persian alone, without borrowing from Arabic. Literally it means the city or country (âbâd) of “no-where” (nâ-kojâ). At first sight, as we have already observed, it seems an exact equivalent of the Greek ou-topia, a word likewise absent from Greek dictionaries, coined by Thomas More as an abstract name for the absence of any location, any situs, within a space our senses can explore and verify. Etymologically, literally, it might therefore be correct to translate Nâ-kojâ-âbâd as outopia.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02135

But in terms of the idea, the intention, and the meaning of the experience itself, that would be a serious misunderstanding. It would repeat the confusion we have already exposed between what is commonly called the imaginary, the unreal, and what our authors have obliged us to distinguish by the technical term imaginal. Such confusion assumes that the imaginative faculty itself has been diminished, along with its object and its power to know. If imagination is identified with mere “fantasy,” then the world it gives form to must inevitably be a utopia, and anyone who trusts this faculty must be a utopian dreamer.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02136

Once the imaginative faculty is no longer governed by a cognitive power precisely situated between two others, that person becomes, potentially, someone who has lost his bearings: paranoid, hallucinating, schizophrenic, and so on. To understand the meaning and reality of Nâ-kojâ-âbâd as something other than a utopia (outopia), we must also recognize that the imaginative faculty—or imaginative consciousness—is something other than a means of producing the imaginary and the unreal.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02137

But this recognition in turn requires a metaphysics of being that makes room for an intermediate level of existence between the world of pure intellect and the world of the senses. By that very fact (eo ipso), such a metaphysics defines the orientation and function of the faculty of knowledge whose proper object is this intermediate world. That level of existence is the Malakût, a world at once spiritual and concrete. We have already seen throughout the investigations presented here how important it is.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02138
It follows that Nâ-kojâ-âbâd cannot mean something without spatial extent, reduced to a point. The word âbâd means a city, a cultivated and inhabited country—something that occupies an expanse.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02139

We must therefore begin by overcoming the old division between what is spiritual and what has extension. What concerns us here is the realm that Islamic theosophical tradition describes as lying “beyond the mountain of Qâf”: the mystical cities of Jâbalqâ, Jâbarsâ, and Hûrqalyâ, which in turn include many others (among them the Green Island and the islands of the five cities). When our authors tell us that the region of these cities begins “at the convex surface of the Sphere of Spheres,” they are offering the clearest possible image of what this means.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02140

Nâ-kojâ-âbâd begins at the point where one “leaves” the Sphere that defines every possible direction in our world, the Sphere upon which the celestial points of the compass are, in principle, inscribed. Once we have crossed that boundary, the question where? (ubi? kojâ?) plainly loses its meaning—or at least the meaning it has within the space of ordinary experience. This is Nâ-kojâ-âbâd: a “place that is not contained within a place,” a place not enclosed by any geographical setting in which the question “where?” could be answered.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02141
But what, precisely, does it mean to leave this “where” behind?
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02142

It cannot mean moving bodily from one location to another, as a physical body moves between places within the same continuous space. Suhrawardi suggests something quite different with his image of a drop of balm passing through to the back of a hand held up toward the sun.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02143

What is involved is a movement inward: entering within, passing through the interior, and in doing so finding oneself outside. The essential relation is between what is outer, visible, and exoteric (ta exô, zâhir) and what is inner, invisible, and esoteric (ta éxô, bâtin). To leave the “where,” the category of ubi, is to pass beyond the outward appearances that enclose hidden inner realities like a shell around a kernel. For the Stranger, the gnostic, it is to come home.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02144

Yet there is something strange about this passage. Once it has taken place, the hidden reality is now what surrounds, embraces, and contains what had previously appeared outer and visible. By turning inward, one has emerged beyond that external reality. It is now immaterial reality that surrounds and contains what we call material reality. Spiritual reality, then, is not located in a “where”; rather, the “where” is within it.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02145

Indeed, spiritual reality is itself the where of everything else. It is therefore not itself situated in a place, and the question where?—the category of ubi—does not apply to it. Its place, its âbâd, is nâ-kojâ, “nowhere,” because its ubi is an ubique: a “where” that is everywhere. Once we grasp this, we have surely grasped what is essential for following the geography of visionary experience and understanding its sense—both its meaning and its direction.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02146

We can also begin to distinguish something crucial: the visionary perceptions of spiritual figures such as Suhrawardi and the traveler to the Green Island from what our modern vocabulary dismisses as inventions, imaginings, or even utopian delusions.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02147

The very idea of an imagination that has “lost its bearings” presupposes a view of the human being that can no longer identify or safeguard the imagination’s proper axis. It is our understanding of the human being that has first lost its mind.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02148

We would do well to reflect on the convergence between the teachings of the masters who shaped the intellectual life of the Islamic East—Avicenna, Suhrawardi, Ibn 'Arabi, Nasir al-Din Tusi, Mulla Sadra Shirazi, and others—and those Western masters whose testimony remains priceless, both for the present and for the future, because it bears witness to precisely what is absent from so-called modern Western thought, at least in its official forms.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02149

In short, can there be a phenomenology of visionary experience—of ek-stasis, a standing outside the space of this world—that does not also account for the experience of coming into this world? Must we not understand departure from this world and arrival in it as two opposite aspects of one and the same phenomenon?
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02150
We find a remarkable beginning of such an account in the work of Nasir al-Din Tusi, the great Shiite thinker profoundly marked by Ismaili esotericism. To come into this world is to “leave paradise.”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02151

But that departure is not a movement from one place to another; it is a change of state. As Tusi explains it, we pass from True Reality (haqîqat) and true meaning (bâtin: the inward, esoteric meaning) into what ordinary consciousness undoubtedly takes to be the only reality, but which, in relation to True Reality, is merely metaphor (majâz). In this way, realities in the truest sense have come to seem doubtful and improbable, suspect and ambiguous.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02152

Conversely, leaving this world and reaching its true meaning does not refer to the biological event of death (which even today specialists cannot agree how to define). The true meaning of life and death is the spiritual meaning of each. The question of survival after death is not an extension of a problem in physics. It arises on the level of a spiritual world whose concrete reality Western philosophy may have lost sight of centuries ago, preferring instead the world of logical concepts. This is why the usual expression that the dead “have departed” is misleading.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02153

Many of those so described were already spiritually dead and have never left this world, because dead souls cannot leave it. To leave this world, then, is to have been reborn with Khidr in the Spring of Life; it is to have become a stranger to the world of ghorbat, of exile—that metaphorical world with which ordinary consciousness is satisfied.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02154

In short, one must first be alive, raised to spiritual life, before one can experience death as an exitus, a departure. For death as exitus means precisely this: the soul leaves this world alive. Ecstasy and visionary experiences are anticipations of that departure. To pass beyond the limits of the cosmos, beyond the highest Sphere, is not to accomplish some feat of space travel, like the cosmonauts of our time. It is above all to pass from spiritual infancy into maturity, to pierce the darkness and attain a true consciousness of True Reality.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02155

A whole body of related testimony could be assembled from the masters of spiritual Protestantism: Valentin Weigel, Jacob Böhme, Gottfried Arnold, and others. In a remarkable passage from 1588, Weigel explains what sacred history—or hierohistory—means when it says that Lucifer left heaven or Adam left paradise. Such an event does not mean being transferred from one location to another.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02156

“Adam, driven out of paradise, remained in the very place where he had been before; for this great universe was his paradise, speaking in the outward sense, just as his inward and heavenly paradise was the Imago Dei, the image of God within him.” We should therefore say: “Hell and paradise are not places. Each person carries paradise and hell within himself. Whoever does not know himself does not know his homeland, which is paradise, the kingdom of God [...]. Our material body is not our true dwelling, since death has the power to drive us out of it.”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02157
But “God in us and we in God: whoever lives in this way truly lives at home, in his homeland, and no one can drive him from it.”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02158

Not even death can drive the gnostic from home, because “in that world” (in jener Welt; Plotinus would have said “there”), there is no natural body made of the elements, occupying a place and looking around itself with bodily eyes. Instead there is “a supernatural heavenly body, a spiritual body,” formed by the Holy Spirit and needing no external place. These declarations are in complete harmony with what our philosophers and spiritual masters have taught us about self-knowledge, the resurrection body, and what it means to “see the Imam in Hûrqalyâ.”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02159

Nâ-kojâ-âbâd is the kingdom of subtle bodies, of “spiritual bodies,” the threshold of the Malakût, the world of the Soul. It begins “at the convex surface of the Sphere of Spheres” because that is the boundary at which the relation expressed by the words in or within is reversed. Spiritual bodies are not in a world—not even their own world—as a material body occupies its place or is contained in another body.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02160

The text of Plotinus that all our thinkers, from Avicenna to Qazi Sa'id Qummi, read and annotated under the title The Theology of Aristotle explains that every spiritual entity is “within the whole Sphere of its heaven.” Each certainly exists independently of the others, yet all exist together, and each is within every other. It would be quite wrong to picture this other world as a featureless, undifferentiated heaven. There is multiplicity, but the relations of spiritual space differ from those of the space beneath the starry heavens as profoundly as being inside a body differs from being “within the whole of one's heaven.”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02161

Thus we can say, with the Theology, that “behind this world there is a Heaven, an Earth, a sea, animals, plants, and heavenly human beings; but every being there is heavenly. The spiritual entities there correspond to the human beings there, yet nothing there is earthly.” All this seems applicable to the marvels and strange phenomena of the Green Island, the islands of the five cities, and the rest.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02162

What is opening here to every visionary experience is, in effect, a quarta dimensio, a fourth dimension. Following our pilgrims, we find ourselves in a world familiar to any reader of the great Swedish visionary and theosopher Emanuel Swedenborg. Like our Shiite theosophers, Swedenborg had probably read the Plotinian work called The Theology of Aristotle; but he speaks above all from his own experience, from things “seen and heard by himself.”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02163

Several of his pages on the nature of spiritual space deserve to be recalled here, so perfectly do they express the essential point. He explains that “although everything in Heaven appears exactly as it does in the world, in a place and in a space, nevertheless the Angels have no notion or idea of place and space.”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02164

For “all movements in the spiritual world are brought about by changes of inward state, so that movements are nothing other than changes of state ... Those who are in a similar state are near one another, and those who are in a dissimilar state are far apart ... Spaces in Heaven are only outward states corresponding to inward states. It is for this reason alone that the Heavens are distinct from one another ... When someone moves from one place to another ... he arrives sooner when he wishes to, and later when he does not; the road itself lengthens or shortens according to his desire ... I have often seen this and have been amazed by it.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02165

“From this it is again clear that distance, and consequently space, depend entirely on the Angels' inward states. And because this is so, the notion or idea of space cannot enter their thought, although spaces exist among them just as they do in the world.”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02166

We could hardly ask for a more exact description of Nâ-kojâ-âbâd, the “eighth clime” and its mysterious cities. We are all the more justified in seeing it this way because we find a precise counterpart in Mulla Sadra Shirazi. The testimony of these two masters leads, in brief, to this conclusion: there is a spiritual place and there is a bodily place, but unlike the latter, the former cannot be identified by answering the question ubi?, “where?”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02167

For anyone who reaches Nâ-kojâ-âbâd, everything is reversed in relation to ordinary perception and consciousness. It is the where, the place, that dwells within the soul; extended bodily substance dwells within spiritual substance, just as the body dwells within the soul and the soul surrounds and sustains the body. A whole metaphysical tradition could be called upon in support of this.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02168

Let us quote these lines from Solomon ibn Gabirol, which sum up the matter particularly well: “The way universal bodily substance resides within universal spiritual substance should be compared to the way the body resides within the soul. Just as the soul surrounds and sustains the body, so universal spiritual substance surrounds and sustains the universal body of the world. And just as the soul is in itself separate from the body of the world, yet attached to it without touching it, so spiritual substance is in itself separate from the body of the world, yet attached to it without touching it.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02169

“We can form an idea of how spiritual substance is joined to bodily substance, and in general of how spiritual substances are joined to one another and exist within one another, by considering how light or fire is joined to air, color and figure to quantity, quantity to substance, and spiritual accidents to spiritual substances. For since visible things must be images of invisible things, the way the different elements of bodily substance [such as color, figure, quantity, and substance] are joined and exist within one another must be an image of how spiritual substances are joined and exist within one another.”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02170

This is why we cannot say where spiritual place is: it is not something situated somewhere but something that gives things their situation. The soul itself is the place. The apparent location, the landscape in which the soul moves, is then the image of an inward place. The ubi of this inward place is also an ubique: its “where” is everywhere.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02171

We cannot enter the soul's place, with its own geography, without a break—sudden or gradual—from geographical coordinates. We saw this, for example, in the account of the journey to the Green Island. The traveler sets out; at a certain point the familiar map of the world ceases to apply.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02172

Yet he is unaware of the precise moment when the break occurs. Only afterward does he realize what has happened, with wonder or unease. If he recognized it as it happened, perhaps he could retrace his route or show it to someone else. As things stand, he can describe where he was, but he cannot tell anyone else where the road runs.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02173

Here we come to something essential: the connection, which we noted again above, between Nâ-kojâ-âbâd as a “place” of the soul and the special role of the imaginative faculty. The organ by which the soul makes its migration, returns ab extra ad intra—from outside to inside—and undergoes this reversal of its sense of place is neither the senses nor pure intellect. It is an intermediate power: active, image-forming Imagination. We have already seen how important it is that Mulla Sadra Shirazi regards Imagination as a purely spiritual faculty, independent of the physical organism and therefore independent of that organism's death: something like the soul's “subtle body.”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02174

We can now better appreciate the consequences of this position. Mulla Sadra's theory of knowledge affirms a union between the perceiving subject and the form perceived, which means that the perceived form becomes inwardly present to the perceiver. This principle holds at all three levels of perception: sensory, imaginative, and intellectual.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02175

Imaginative perception and imaginative consciousness therefore possess their own genuine power of knowledge, directed toward the world that belongs to them: the 'âlam al-mithâl, the mundus imaginalis, or imaginal world. This is the world of mystical cities such as Hûrqalyâ, where time can be reversed and space takes its shape from desire, because space is nothing but the outward aspect of an inward state. It is not yet the world of the pure cherubic Intelligences (Jabarût), nor the world of Platonic Ideas. It is the Malakût, the world of the Soul.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02176

Imagination is thus firmly aligned between two other powers of knowing. Its own world stands in symbolic relation to the worlds belonging to those other powers. This relation provides a kind of safeguard against Imagination running wild, allowing it to perform its rightful function: bringing about the events narrated in visionary accounts such as Suhrawardi's.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02177

Every approach to Nâ-kojâ-âbâd takes place through the imaginative faculty, through a concrete “realism” peculiar to imaginative consciousness. This helps explain the extraordinary seriousness of the Persian mystical epic, from Attar to Jami and Nur Ali Shah, which continually unfolds the same archetypes in new symbols. For Imagination to lose its axis, to run unchecked and cease performing its task of producing symbols that lead toward inward meaning, its proper world—the mundus imaginalis, the domain of the Malakût—must first have disappeared.
